Photograph: Felix Andler View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas’s case has raised concerns over Sweden’s hardline approach to the EU-UK withdrawal agreement. Photograph: Felix Andler Brexit ‘This is hell’: British widow ‘sick’ with worry after losing Brexit deportation appeal Joyce Thomas, 78, faces being forced to leave Sweden after 21 years in growing row over country’s approach to EU withdrawal British widow, 78, told to leave Sweden under Brexit rules Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The 78-year-old British widow threatened with removal from Sweden after 21 years has said she has been left feeling sick with worry after being told she had lost an appeal against deportation in a growing row over the country’s handling of Brexit. “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong. I don’t take anything from this country. I am self sufficient, I put money in this country, have no criminal record,” said Joyce Thomas from her home in Sweden on Thursday. Her plight, first revealed by the Guardian, has raised concerns in Brussels and in the UK about Sweden’s approach to the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was supposed to protect British nationals who lived in an EU member state before Brexit. Earlier this week another family told how their father, a dementia patient in full-time care, was also threatened with removal after 25 years in Sweden. The administrative court in Luleå upheld Sweden’s migration agency decision that Thomas was not eligible to stay because her application was made in 2023, after the cut-off date of December 2021. Her legal representatives told the court in Luleå it was “not proportionate for her to be deported solely because she missed a deadline due to insufficient information. Furthermore, it is not acceptable that the Swedish authorities failed to inform her that she needed to file an application and of the deadline by which it was to be filed.” View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas faces being given four weeks to leave Sweden, separating her from her son, grandchildren and network of friends. Photograph: Copyright: Felix Andler/TheGuardian Thomas now faces the prospect of a letter from the migration agency giving her four weeks to leave voluntarily , separating her from her son, her grandchildren, her network of friends, and away from her husband’s grave, which she regularly visits. If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and “registered on a watchlist” preventing entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Sweden votes to back laws reinforcing its immigration crackdown Read more “No circumstances have come to light that would lead to a determination that, in your situation, you are particularly vulnerable,” the court ruling said noting that she had lived most of her life in the UK, had a pension from the UK and another son in the UK. Thomas argued that after 21 years all her support network was in Sweden, with 23 people including doctors, priests and friends and fellow churchgoers writing to testify in support of her case. “My friends, my husband’s burial place, grandchildren, everything is here, and to have to go and start again, it’s just unbelievable that at my age I’ve got to be uprooted for my home,” she said. “This is hell. I get up in the morning, it’s in my head, I go to bed at night, it’s in my head. It’s horrible. I mean I have done nothing wrong. I am self sufficient. I put money in the country. I don’t take money out. I can’t comprehend this,” she added. Her husband died in 2023 from cancer just four months after his last trip back to the UK to visit family. It was on the return that he learned from border officials that they had to make a special application to stay after Brexit . Under article 18 of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, late applications are permissible if there are “reasonable grounds” for doing so. David Milstead, of the grassroots campaign group British in Sweden, said: “It would be difficult to find anyone who would argue that what is happening to Mrs Thomas and others in Sweden was an intended outcome of the withdrawal agreement. Problems will inevitably emerge when a new treaty is put into practice. However, the UK, EU and Sweden must act to address them. Words and expressions of concern won’t cut it.” While the migration agency said not knowing an application was needed was not a “reasonable ground” for granting post-residency rights, Thomas is adamant neither she or her husband were notified that an application needed to be made before the end of 2021. “The Swedish authorities have our ID cards, they have our emails, we heard nothing,” said Thomas. In Berlin Pride Attack Exposes Europe’s Changing Terrorism Threat, The Media Line’s Giorgia Valente examines the difficulty of identifying when extremist online activity crosses the line into operational intent. Investigators say 21-year-old Abdul Ballout drove a van into a crowd before continuing on foot with a machete, killing a Polish woman and injuring at least 29 others. German prosecutors later said they recovered a video in which a masked individual believed to be Ballout pledged allegiance to the Islamic State (ISIS). (AFP File Photo) by Deutsche Presse-Agentur - dpa Aug 18, 2026 5:48 pm Edited By Nurbanu Tanrıkulu Kızıl A large-scale cyberattack targeting Latvia's Road Traffic Safety Directorate (CSDD) has compromised data linked to 1.2 million individuals and 200,000 companies, the agency said Tuesday. The attack reportedly secured information last week such as first and last names, payment details, vehicle licence plates and the address registered on the day the service was provided. Latvia has a population of around 1.9 million. It was initially unclear who was behind the incident. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said that a cyberattack originating from another country could not be ruled out, according to the Leta news agency. Latvia's cybersecurity authority and the CSDD warned that the stolen data could be misused by fraudsters. Kulbergs ordered an investigation into the incident and criticized the CSDD management for informing him about the data theft only after a delay. "I have to say that I am unpleasantly surprised by a certain IT-security infantilism that exists in some regulatory authorities and government institutions," the prime minister said. He referred to a previous hacker attack on the state forestry administration in June. Two "serious cyber incidents" occurring within a short period were a clear signal that additional security measures were needed, he said. Photograph: Jenny Kane/AP View image in fullscreen Federal officials have urged recipients to treat the mail as ‘potentially hazardous’. Photograph: Jenny Kane/AP US midterm elections 2026 FBI investigates letters with ‘unknown substance’ sent to US election officials Election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma receive a powdery substance, prompting evacuations Ariana Baio and agencies Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.06 EDT First published on Thu 15 Oct 2026 13.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance”. Just weeks before November’s US midterm elections , election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma received envelopes containing a powdery substance, leading to evacuations. A similar package containing white powder was also sent to the Ohio secretary of state, but the US Postal Service intercepted the package. The US Senate sergeant at arms, who serves as chief law enforcement for the Senate, informed members of the upper chamber on Thursday of the investigation in a message, obtained by the Associated Press. The notice said law enforcement officials were working to intercept additional mail, but it is possible some could reach their destination. Federal authorities have urged recipients to treat the mail as “potentially hazardous”. Brendan Donahue, a senior official with the US Postal Inspection Service, confirmed the investigation into the suspicious mailings during a press conference on Thursday. “We are committed to protecting our nation’s election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable,” Donahue said. The US Postal Inspection Service referred the Guardian to the FBI. In a statement, the FBI said it would not confirm specific instances but said that it was “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State office and their related election officers” alongside the US Postal Inspection Service. “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.” The FBI declined to comment on what the purported substance may have been. In Oklahoma , state troopers determined the substance mailed to the Oklahoma state capitol complex was non-hazardous. In Cook county, Illinois, an envelope containing only white powder was sent to Maria Pappas, the treasurer, on Thursday morning, prompting a response from local emergency responders and law enforcement. The powder turned out to be baking powder, Pappas’s office confirmed to the Guardian. “Unfortunately, one-tenth of 1% of the population causes 100% of the problems: crimes, threats, murders, beatings and abusiveness, etc. Too bad that normal folk have to have their guard up when a minority of folk lash out with their craziness,” Pappas said in a statement. Another letter containing an unknown substance was sent to the Pennsylvania state department but intercepted by the USPS, Votebeat reported Thursday. Two organizations representing secretaries of state and state election directors released a joint statement raising alarm at the mail containing the unknown substance. The National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) “are deeply concerned by these incidents”, the organizations wrote in a statement on Wednesday. “As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy,” they wrote. “Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.” Other officials have received mail containing suspicious substances, including Chris Murphy, the Democratic senator from Connecticut. The letter was sent to his Hartford office, according to NBC. Alex Padilla, the senator from California, was also the target of a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by the USPS. Similar incidents have arisen during election cycles in the country. During the 2024 election, at least 14 election offices across the country had received mail containing white powder. In some cases, the substance turned out to be flour. In 2023, election offices in six states also received mail containing white powder. In some cases, the powder contained trace amounts of fentanyl, a powerful opioid.
